utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you have requested that your name and identity be not released to the public and the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now for the record I would ask the usher to show you a piece of paper with your name on it. Would you please, without stating your name, just tell us whether you recognise your actual name on this leaf of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then may I ask the usher to hand over this piece of paper to the Registry officer to be available for anybody to be sure about the identity of the witness inside this court room. So, sir, you will thus be known as Mr. N; all right? Can you please tell us: what is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can tell us what kind of schools did you attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished as a machinist and then I also worked in the restaurant industry and I completed training for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live at the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Viniste in the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Viniste a village with Serbian or Muslim or Croatian majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Viniste was a hamlet where Croats and Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the majority of Serbs or Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 14 Serbian households and three Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Can you say approximately how many kilometres -- I mean, the distance between Viniste and Konjic town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5, 5 and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, was there a time when Viniste was affected by any armed conflict in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no armed conflict, but on 19th May 1992 the Croatian-Muslim forces moved towards Cerici and Bjelovcina, passing through this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say in which day did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was starting on 19th May until -- and it went on until 23rd May while I was still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested on May 23rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain the circumstances of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was unarmed. I was at home. The members of the TO arrived. That was the Muslim military. Myself and some 10, 12 people -- I don't know the exact number -- we were taken to Konjic, where they brought us in front of a motel. However, that day on the initiative of a Croatian we were returned to the village of Viniste, because down there we were told that we were not guilty of anything, that we were not arrested for carrying arms, so we were returned. Emir Alijic, who was the Commander of the military in the adjoining village of Homolje, also Sejo Didik, the driver, they returned us there and we sat there, but Esad said that we should move to Homolje, to this Muslim village, because there were big manoeuvres in that area, military manoeuvres, and for our safety we should do that. I think he expressed a desire to protect us. However, on that same day, when we were moved to the village of Homolje from where I was, that same evening the police arrived and they were composed of the HVO and the TO members. There were eight of them, and myself, Branko and Jordan Gotovac were taken to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any weapon at the time of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any armed group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in any way take part in the defence of the village of Viniste?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no defence there at all. For a while -- in fact, before that, before they attacked, the surrounding villages, Donje Selo, Cerici and Bjelovcina, we had watches together with the Croatians, but we were also linked with the Muslims from the Homolje village. So there was nothing hidden. Everything was known. The intentions were clear. The intention was to protect the village and to protect the hamlet. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you said you were brought to Celebici. Approximately at what time did you arrive at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought to Celebici on 23rd May 1992. I cannot recall the exact time, but it was already dark, so I don't know what time it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners were together with you when you were transported -- with which transportation means were you transported to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought in a van. I don't know the make of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners were together with you in that van which transported you to Celebici on May 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko Gotovac and his son Jordan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before going ahead with your account, can you now tell the court: how long was your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Celebici between 23rd May until 31st August 1992, after which I was transferred to the sports hall in Musala, in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, going back to your account, what happened to you right after your arrival at Celebici on May 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 23rd May, when I was brought to Celebici, after I got out of this van that brought us there, we were taken in front of what was the command building, after which they were taking us into an office and taking down our information, and then they took us to the Hangar Number 22, and there were some 30-40 people from Donje Selo, Bjelovcina and Cerici there. Since it was the night, only the next day I figured out that this was the number of people that were there. After that, on 24th May, in the morning I was taken out of the hangar. Almir Nujic was a policeman. At that time he was wearing a white belt, so I assumed that he was a policeman. So he took me out and took me to the administration building where there was a mess hall. There were seven or eight people in uniform. At that time they started asking me certain questions and these questions had nothing to do with me, but Bato Alikadic started beating me the first with a cable in the area of the head. I fell down. He continued beating me after I fell to the floor, and there was Almir Nujic, who was also taking part in that. He was kicking me in the rib cage area, the kidney area and head area and then my jaw cracked at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, please slow down in your account, because the interpreters have to keep up. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time two teeth were knocked out and several others were cracked. That beating lasted some half an hour, after which they threw me back into the Hangar Number 22, where I could not get up for several days. I could not open my mouth to take any food. Also there was not enough food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why could you not open your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably because my jaw was cracked and I could not open my mouth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. N, excuse me for a moment. Before going ahead in your account, I would like you to clarify something again about your very evening of your arrival at Celebici. You say you entered Building Number 22 and there were other people there. Was any of these people inside Building 22 familiar to you and can you mention any of their names, when you arrived there in the evening of May 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised Danilo Gotovac, Mirko Babic. I knew some people from Cerici, Mladen Golubovic, for instance. I also found the late Zeljko Klimenta. So there were ... I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the people? Are you in a position to mention other ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could, but there were people from Donje Selo, Cedo Cecez. I can't recollect all the names right now, but I knew all these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. As far as you could observe, which were the physical conditions of the prisoners inside Building 22 when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night I could not notice anything. It was night-time, and the next day I recognised these people. For instance, Slobodan Babic, who was sort of beside himself. He could not even speak. He was just uttering screams. He was immobile. He could not get up. After that, a day or two later, Radoslav Kuljanin was brought in and Milivoje Kuljanin, also from Donje Selo. Milivoje Kuljanin had cuts on his head and later I heard -- he told me that he received 20 blows with beer bottles on his head, on his forehead, and Kuljanin had swollen areas around his eyes, and he could not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, did these injured people inside Building 22 receive any medical care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until that point, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they treated in the following days inside building 22?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How long was he there in Building Number 22.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him how long he was there in Building Number 22 and then ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. I can ask you that immediately. How long did you stay in Building Number 22, Mr. N?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 13 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to these injured people, how was Slobodan Babic treated in the following days inside Number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Babic -- since I was not there when he was brought in; I was brought in later -- but from the people I heard later that on the way to Celebici Slobodan Babic had been beaten, and I even heard that they had pushed the rifle inside -- the barrel of the rifle inside his mouth and injured him. So he was half dead when I got there. One night they brought him out of the hangar and he spent the night outside of the Hangar Number 22 and the next day another prisoner and myself came out to clean up where he had lain. Later I heard from Dr. Relja Mrkajic that Slobodan Babic died in the Third March School in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment. I am sorry to interrupt your cross-examination. This has nothing to do with this witness. I have a message from Mr. Landzo who says he is feeling very sick. He needs to be excused from the court room. Could we take a fifteen-minute break? I do not know whether it is appropriate but I need to inform the Trial Chamber that he is feeling very ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What do the rules say? Can we hold the trial in his absence for fifteen minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would have to look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have a look at the rule, if you want to. Please check up the rule. I do not know about the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will have a break for fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please check the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will look at the rule. Thank you. (3.15 pm) (Short break) (3.31 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we bring the witness in? Ms. McMurrey, I hope we are all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we have a small problem that can be reconciled. He is not feeling very well right now and Mr. Moran looked up the statute for me. I don't believe that we can go forward in the trial without him unless he waives that. This is a very important witness. I believe we can go forward right now if I could just have a word with Mr. Hocking just for one second. I was trying to do that when you all knocked to come in. If I could just have one second to speak to Mr. Hocking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your interpretation is subject to some other considerations too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are standing here, Judge Jan asked the question on what do the rules and the statutes say. I could not find a word in the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is nothing directly on this. There is a rule 18 which gives conditions under which --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Article 21, section 4D of the statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will look at our rules. 18 gives circumstances but definitely, I agree, it does not control this on control of proceedings. It does not completely cover it. I think you can carry on with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Now, Mr. N, maybe I was not quite clear with my last question, so I will repeat the question for you. I wanted to know, as far as you can have seen, how was Slobodan Babic treated in the following days inside Building 22, after your arrival there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw when uniformed people came in, though he was half dead, they continued hitting him. That is what I saw. Several times they hit him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you said he died. Do you mean you could see his dead body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I thought he was dead when they took him out of the hangar and he spent the night there, but Relja Mrkajic told us later that officially he died in the elementary school, Third March, in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So since we are talking about the Building Number 22, could you please describe briefly the physical characteristics of this Building Number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Building 22 was the shelter of the fire brigade. There were some pumps inside and I don't know what. I don't know exactly how long it was. There were 40 people -- when there were 40 people inside it was very crowded, and you couldn't lie down full length on the concrete where we were lying, because there were a lot of us, so that we were rather cramped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the life conditions in Number 22 as far as water, drinking water and food were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us out occasionally to the administrative building, where there was a toilet, and that was when we could drink water. Occasionally somebody managed to bring in a bottle of water. Anyway, we had small quantities of water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Small quantities. Food was distributed or rather a loaf of bread was cut into 18 pieces. So for three meals we had a piece of bread for each meal. On several occasions they threw us some liver paste, but these were very small quantities for so many people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Liver paste?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Liver paste.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Paste?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Liver paste. What happened about toilet facilities when you were not brought outside. Were there any toilet facilities inside hangar 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were none in 22. We were mostly taken out to the administrative building to use the WC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were you taken out of that for toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three times during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to the account you were giving to us about the next morning, you told us about the beating you suffered the next morning. Could you tell us which were the physical conditions of yours when this beating was over in the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten up. I couldn't stand. The guard dragged me to the doors of hangar 22, where I was taken over by the prisoners, who put me in the corner, where my place was. I couldn't stand up for several days and they would carry me to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you eat in the following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Jordan Gotovac would give me some food with his finger and Zeljko Klimenta, the late Zeljko Klimenta, somehow managed to get some milk and he would pour a few drops into my mouth. Anyway, I could not put anything into my mouth myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you told us that you remained in Building Number 22 during about 13 days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated in the following days after that? Did you personally suffer any other physical maltreatment after that during your stay in Building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One day, I think it was 27th May, when they were bringing in people from Bradina, Midhat Pirkic, who had his own group, they took me out in front of 22 and one of his soldiers hit me several times in the ribs and the kidneys, and on that occasion I saw people leaning up against the wall at the entrance to the camp, where the building was, and I saw these men propped up against the wall, being beaten up and forced to use Muslim religious greetings and Croatian greetings too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said these people came from Bradina. How do you know that these people came from Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because the guards kept saying that they were going to Bradina, that they would bring people from Bradina. They even said they would release us when they brought them in and that is how I knew. Several days later we met those people in Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge of who were the people who maltreated these people at the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know their names exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that was on May 27. Can you tell us at what time of the day did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, because I was half conscious on that day, but I saw this and I learned later that it was 27th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long could you eyewitness that scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between five and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any reason, as far as you know, why you were called out and beaten in that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. N, did you stay in any other building inside the detention camp after being for about 13 days in Building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, did you stay in any other building other than Building 22 inside the camp after those 13 days you spent in Number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After those 13 days I was transferred to Hangar Number 6 and before that I was taken across to -- across from Building Number 22 to the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what reason were you brought to the administration building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us there for questioning. They took us to clean those premises, the toilets, some bedrooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that you were brought to Hangar 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. He is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, he said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He said that. Okay. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: First he was taken to the administration block, then he was made to clean the toilet and make up bedrooms, then taken to Hangar Number 6. That is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the reason for which you were transferred from 22 to Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of what was Building 22 used for after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards the people who were arrested were there: Dr. Relja Mrkajic, Petko Grubac, and they brought in prisoners there who were beaten up, wounded. When they inflicted burns on them, then they were taken there for some aid to be given to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now describe the physical characteristics of Building Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. I think it was about 25 metres long and about 13 metres wide. This is a rough estimate, of course. We didn't have any way to measure the building, but that is my assessment. Around it was metal sheeting and below the roof there was the steel structure carrying the roof. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many doors did Hangar 6 have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let us say how many doors normally used were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Hangar 6 have any window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were two small windows, but we never had any cause to look through those windows, any possibility to look through those windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply, when we were brought there we were allowed only to look in front of us and to stay in the place allotted to us. I was turned with my back towards those windows when I was brought into that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those windows high or low, I mean the position on the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I did not get your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were high up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, how long did you stay inside this Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed until 31st August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did every prisoner have a given position inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say how were the prisoners distributed inside Number 6; I mean, how were their positions organised inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two rows right next to the walls, two rows in the middle and up at the top of the hangar; in other words, we were lined up in a circle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you personally maintain the same position during the whole period inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. First, I sat in the middle row, right from the entrance, and then I was moved towards the top of the middle row to the left, towards the end of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. May I now ask that the witness be provided with Prosecution Exhibit number 1, page 7, which is the map we already have in evidence, and can it be placed in the ELMO, please, or maybe simply a photocopy of this so we can have the witness exactly mark his two positions inside the hangar? Can it be placed in the ELMO, please? All right. Can you recognise this map as the map of Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate -- please do not look at the video. Look on your right-hand side in the very piece of paper there. Can you indicate on that map the door of the hangar on the map, just indicate with your finger, if you wish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please indicate on this map your two different positions inside Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the permission of the court, may I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You might have some difficulty, because there were two rows in the middle, and he says he was sitting to begin with in the middle row near the door, then in the middle row towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly. So I would like him to be provided with a pen and mark more or less exactly the two different positions in which -- may I ask -- yes, you have a pen. Could you please observe carefully this map and then mark with an X your first position. Is this your first position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please write "1" beside this mark? Would you now please mark with an X your second position on the map and would you please write "2" beside this second mark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is correct. So we have position number 1, which is close to the door, and position number 2 on this other point here. Thank you. Mr. N, was there any particular reason for which you changed position inside Hangar 6 from position 1 to position 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say: approximately when did you change position inside the hangar? When did you move from position number 1 to position number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly after a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us say: in which position did you stay longer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. The answer is not coming.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which position he occupied from one stage to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The answer did not come in the transcript. He did actually give an answer but I did not see it, so I will repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know how much time I spent in those positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not asking you a very precise answer. I would like to know whether you spent more time in position number 1 or more time in position number 2, or approximately the time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly half/half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this comparison? Has it anything to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The relevance is to see what he eyewitnessed exactly from these two positions in the following part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It does not matter if he was in a particular position. He must still witness if he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I will come now to this point. From your first position could you see outside of the door when the door was open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of the camp would be visible through the open door with that first position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see maybe three or four metres outside the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your second position? From your second position could you see outside of the door when the door was open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I could just see the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the relevance for these questions, your Honour, just to see what he might eyewitness from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is your case. When there is a particular example or cause and you want to ask him a question as to where he was sitting, it would be obvious whether he could see from there or he cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Of course. We found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not need to separate into times or places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We found out what he could see outside from the first position and he could not see anything outside from the second position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is the relevance of my questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not introduce the second part. If he was sitting behind, how can he see?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there are no objections, I would like to tender this photocopy of the map of Hangar 6 for admission. It should be Prosecution Exhibit Number 93, if I am not wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is already tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If it is necessary, it would be more convenient if you draw the middle line also, showing the middle rows also, so we know exactly. He has indicated the places, but instead of having just the walls, if you also have the middle rows, if they were indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We can invite then the witness to add on the map this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He can draw those lines and then fix his position. This will be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is a document. You do not need to tender it. Show it to him so he can indicate what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If you are in a position to indicate with your pen the rows along which the prisoners were sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So I tender this as Exhibit Number 93, if there are no objections to admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have no objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I may be allowed, this is evidence Number 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry. So I was wrong. Thank you. 92. Sir, how were the conditions like in Number 6? I mean, drinking water, for instance; let us start with drinking water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Number 6 there was a shortage of water. In front of the hangar there was a tube, but we couldn't drink water when we wanted. For a time water was brought into the hangar and distributed to us -- how can I explain that -- in very small quantities. It was the summer. It was hot. The walls were steel, so we lacked water. We didn't have enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again we had a piece of bread in the morning, at midday and in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that has been asked and answered. Was that asked and answered already about the slice -- 18 slices on the bread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Even so I think it does not matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then he was talking about room Number 22. Now he is talking about Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In Hangar Number 22 they were getting three slices of bread, morning, afternoon, night. Now in Hangar Number 6, he wants to find out there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is this all your answer about food in Number 6, Mr. N?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the toilet facilities, if any, in the period of time when you were in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The toilet was behind the hangar. There were two holes dug up where people went to relieve themselves during the day and during the night a bucket would be put inside near the door, where people would relieve themselves during the night in this bucket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go to these toilets whenever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was a time set for that, and people went there in groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the sleeping facilities? How did you sleep in Hangar 6? Did you have any blankets or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we slept on concrete. Underneath those who had put their jackets or something, and we would lie on that. Again those who managed to find something would have a piece of blanket for those who managed to find one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners did you observe being in Hangar 6 when you first arrived in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, how many they were when we arrived, but I think that the number was somewhere around 280 all told in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this number have any variations during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it did vary, because some people were killed and then normally they would be carried out of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were any of these prisoners being there familiar to you? Can you mention any names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The names of the people who were there or who were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us say people who were there in Hangar Number 6 when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people -- when we arrived there were people from Bradina there. I knew some of them. Some of them I did not. I could name some names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Tell us some names, the names you can recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were Nedzo Samoukovic; his father, Bosko; Vukasin Mrkajic; Pero Mrkajic and his brother Bosko, Zoran Djordjic and his father Milan; Brano Djordjic; Stevan Kuljanin; Stevo Gligorevic; Jovo Kuljanin; Savo Miljanic, Damjan Gligorevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I am not asking you to say. Now did you personally suffer any physical maltreatment during your stay in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that happen once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe in detail every single incident, if possible in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 15th July 1992 Esad Landzo, called Zenga, took me out of the hangar. He put a gas mask on my face and he took me behind the adjoining hangar and he ordered me to sit down. I sat down. I didn't know what was coming and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very slowly, Mr. N, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point I saw a knife, which he held in his hand, and this knife was heated. He first took my left hand and started burning me and he made three burns on the left hand. Then afterwards he preheated the knife again and moved to the right hand. After that he heated the knife again and he started burning me on my left leg, on the bare skin, and after which he burnt me with a heated knife on my thighs through the track suit which was synthetic, and while the synthetic burned, the burn widened. After that in front of this hangar he kicked me, even though at that time because the pain of the burns was predominant, I did not feel those blows as much. Then he took a piece of chain and he hit me on my neck with it. Then he ordered me to go back to the hangar, but there were railroad tracks next to the fence there, and some --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow down please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And some girls, some younger girls appeared there at that point. So those young girls walked by and he called me back to come towards those girls. Then he ordered me to kneel. He kicked me a few times and ordered me to graze the grass. After that he ordered me to go back towards the hangar, but he started following me and he took -- how shall I explain it -- he took a fistful of clover and put it in my mouth. I ate some of it. Some of it fell down. After that he ordered me to drink water. Through this fear I could not feel the pain any more and then I entered into the hangar and people said: "Oh, you fared quite well, because you were not screaming, but at this point the blisters were already forming and I showed them what happened to me, but I wasn't the only victim of this. Several other people later in that way --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. N. We need to clarify some points about this incident. You were talking at the beginning of this account about a mask, but it was not quite clear what happened with this mask. Can you explain better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I think that this mask was used so that I could not scream, because the screw on the mask was turned so when I would try to scream, but when I would scream, I would start suffocating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who put this mask on your face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see through the mask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could only see in front of me where I was walking and also I was afraid at that time, and I was wondering what was going to happen to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you breathe normally through the mask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because the screw was screwed on. I had a feeling at that time while I had the mask on my face and when he was burning me with the heated knife that my eyes were popping out and there was no help. I could not breathe air. I have simply started suffocating at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the mask taken off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mask was taken off when he stopped burning me with the knife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he", who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think of Zenga, Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did take the mask off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the incident of the clover? Did that happen right after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, yes. First he ordered me to graze grass and after that he forced me to eat clover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical treatment after this torture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time no; only several days later, because those burns already started to fester because in the hangar there was also dust, and all this festered and it was starting to smell, and I could not -- and after that several days I went to the infirmary. I was taken there, Number 22, where the doctors were, doctors Relja Mrkajic and Petko Grubac. There they tried to offer me some assistance, but they didn't have enough, so they were only able to bandage, and it still hurt terribly. Then the wounds would reopen. There was blood. They were haemorrhaging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this incident did anybody enquire on what had happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were enquiries, but that was more like a provocation, because before that people would complain about what happened to them, but they would even get beaten for that, so we couldn't talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say more precisely what do you mean with enquiries being provocations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because if somebody said something hurt them or they were beaten -- nobody dared say they were beaten up to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did anybody actually ask -- did anybody enquire who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked by Hazim Delic on one occasion. He asked me what happened to me, but I didn't dare tell him, because I was afraid, because then he forced me to tell him what happened to me. In fact, before that he said: "Did Zenga play with you?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. N. Can you describe the following incident concerning you in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One evening -- in fact, that evening some 22 people were taken out in front of the hangar, where they were beaten, and I was fifth or sixth. This was within the period of about half an hour. I was beaten with a wooden object and Esad Landzo, Zenga, took me out and took me -- in fact, he took me behind Hangar Number 6, so the right of the door, and hit me a few times until I fell down to the ground, and on that occasion there were some four or five persons. Some were holding me and the others were beating me from my head to toe with wooden objects that looked like a baseball bat. After that I was thrown through the door into the hangar, and I couldn't go any further. I fell down and Danilo Gotovac approached me and took me to the place where I was lying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, just a moment. Excuse me. You said other persons were there. Can you say who were the other persons present or taking part in this incident??

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The persons who were with Esad Landzo who beat me were unknown to me in that moment. In fact, I couldn't see them, because on that occasion I also had the mask over my head, and it was covered with a white cloth, but when I was brought out of the hangar I noticed Hazim Delic next to the tin wall. He was probably watching it all while they beat me, until I was put the mask over my head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who placed the gas mask over your face in this second occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, could you see through the mask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was a cloth over the mask, a white cloth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how could you see that white cloth was put over the mask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I felt, because I first saw when he came -- when he held the mask and the cloth in his hands, and then after he put the mask on, then he put the cloth afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took off the mask from your face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the mask was taken off from your face, again could you observe whether other people were around you, watching, or anyway present at this incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already answered that. Delic was there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Before the mask; now I am saying after the mask was taken off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my mask was taken off I could not see anything any more, because I was beaten up, and Esad Landzo threw me in there and I fell down at the very entrance and I stayed there until Danilo Gotovac arrived and carried me to the place where I lay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge concerning why you in particular were selected for this kind of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a while ago that other people were taken out from Hangar 6 and you were the sixth maybe or something like that. Do you know anything about what happened to the other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were beaten up a similar way that night with wooden shovel handles or I do not know what else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the second incident did you receive any medical care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I lay a few days. I couldn't move. I urinated uncontrollably and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. N. Can you now describe the following incident, if any, concerning you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When the Red Cross visited, they came into the hangar and we told them everything, what was done to us, and we showed it. I showed our wounds, our bodily wounds that we had. However, as soon as the Red Cross left the hangar, they were not out of the gate, Hazim Delic arrived with eight guards and he arranged them four for every two rows and all prisoners got several hits in the back and the kidney area, and then after that in Hangar Number 6 Hazim Delic personally beat me in front of everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say that this happened following the Red Cross visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this cover all the incidents you suffered personally during the period you stayed in Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. On one occasion when Esad Landzo took out Branko Gotovac in front of the hangar he called in turn Danilo and Jordan, his sons, and he beat them there. Then he brought out me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. He just said he was taken outside the hangar and he was testifying what was occurring outside the hangar. At that point he has no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sorry. He is accounting something about his own experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He just said something before he was outside. Once he is outside too then he can testify about what he saw. I think he just testified about something that happened or occurred outside the hangar that he had no personal knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it was within his personal knowledge. Ask him anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My question was: please talk about this other incident you suffered personally. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard your question and I am answering it as it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found Branko Gotovac outside the hangar. His sons Danilo and Jordan, whom Zenga had called out. He hit him at the gate with a plank on the back and in front of me he beat both Branko and Danilo. On that occasion he took my right hand and a match and he stuck it under my thumb nail. After that it festered and I had terrible pains, and the nail dropped off, and a new nail can still not grow normally. It comes up to a certain size and then it grows thick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you say approximately when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the date. A lot of time has gone by since, and all the things that happened to me I would like to forget as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. N. Does this cover all the incidents you personally suffered? Is there anything else you suffered besides what you told us till now? I am talking about the period you stayed in Hangar 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other incidents. They would take me out and hit me a couple of times, but I didn't pay any attention to that after all the things that I had gone through. So I don't want to go into the minor details. I think what I have said is sufficient regarding what I experienced and what is still visible on my body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now let us come to this. Can you describe now in some detail the physical consequences which are still visible or may be checked on your body after these incidents you personally suffered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have scars from burns on my hands and on both legs. On the left I have two burns and on the right leg, one, which are visible. On my left hand I have two scars which can also be seen well. Another has recovered. On the right hand you can see at least three scars. The others have healed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your jaw suffer any consequences visible today or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My jaw was cracked. It probably healed but at the time I felt pain for a long time and I couldn't swallow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you loose any teeth?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to have to object to his leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already said when he was first taken to room Number 22 he was given a beating with cables and with other objects. His jaw was broken. His teeth were knocked out. His teeth were broken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He could not open his mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Counsel is merely asking him: are there any consequences still visible of that beating. I think it is quite a relevant question. It is not a leading question in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can see my broken teeth. I had broken ribs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't list all the things that happened to me. Virtually everything that could have been damaged was damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you report these broken ribs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, is that referable to a specific incident among the ones you described, the broken ribs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened whenever I was heavily beaten. Each of those heavy beatings had that consequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, some days ago we filed a joint request together with the defence for the medical examination of this witness, the injuries of Mr. N which may still be checked in his body, but in the meantime we have some photos, some pictures taken of these visible injuries, which we handed over already to the defence. If there are no objections, we would like to tender these photos as exhibits, but since Witness N is protected, we should avoid to show, on the ELMO at least, the photos where his face is visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just ask that we -- we have received a copy of the photos, but we would also like to examine his injuries personally to see if they compare to the photos before they are admitted into evidence or shown to the Chamber, if you do not mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you are going to have a medical examination, then why have the photographs exhibited? You have the medical report. You want to show these scars. When you are going to have a joint request for a medical examination, why bring the photographs in? The doctor will tell us: "These scars are still available."

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We agreed on that. I am just saying that we have anyway in the meantime some photos and I might tender them as exhibits if there are no objections and if the Chamber agrees on that; otherwise we will be happy to wait for the medical report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel wants to inspect the injury herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are not doctors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, but I would like to see if they reflect what he has claimed they reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When there is a medical report, that will show everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you want to enjoy his body have, a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then we might not have any objections to the admission of the photographs if they are the same as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it is a joint request made by both of you, what are you arguing about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The medical examination was a joint request. The photographs were not part of our request, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They become unnecessary if you get the medical report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he is going to offer the photographs, we would like to compare them with the actual thing. If he is not going to offer the photographs, then I will sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is up to you. If you want to get them, go and see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Since we probably do not have now the result of the medical examination yet, then maybe everybody in this room might find interesting to watch the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You waste too much time. Go and inspect his legs or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Satisfy yourself that he has those injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are the scars on thighs which require a kind of undressing of the witness. This is the reason why I prefer to take some photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When he was giving the evidence, I knew what it was coming up to. That is why I say if you want to go and see him, she should go and do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If the medical report does not support those injuries, then those photographs become useless. When the medical report shows all the scars, you do not need the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Actually the prosecution does not need actually the photographs. It was our care to have these scars visible to the court in case defence lawyers and first of all the Chamber should want to immediately. Otherwise we have not any difficulty in waiting for the medical report. I will withdraw the photographs your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am leaving it to you. If you have a medical examination now, why have the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am withdrawing the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then I am sparing him his thighs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: His evidence was quite plain. It was his thighs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The medical examination was done and the report is going to come quite soon certainly. Right. Now, anyway, your Honour, I would ask you to allow me to proceed for a short while in private session, since the next question will regard another protected witness, and the events concerning this protected person have been described already by two witnesses previously, but without mentioning the person's name. So we now think that this name should be made available to -- should be made available to the court for the record. So this is why I am asking for a short private session for the next question, if you do not mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: About the brothers?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the names of these people should be made available to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They were made available to the court at one stage by Ms. McMurrey but anyway they were redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If we do that in private session, it will be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you found that the engineers will take care of it? Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed in private session now? Okay. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, did you personally eyewitness any other mistreatment of any other prisoner while you were in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mirko Babic, who came in with his leg burning. I saw Vukasin Mrkajic, who also had fuse wound round his whole body and lit. I saw Bendjo, who was poured with gas and lit. This gas was lit and his track suit was still burning when he came to the hangar. I saw Nedjelko Draganic, who came in also with his leg burning. I saw Momir Kuljanin who had burns on his palm, the palm of his hand. I saw Mirko Djordjic, whose tongue Esad Landzo had burnt with pincers and other beatings that had occurred in front of all the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going into more details, could you say if you eyewitnessed partly or totally who did all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally saw when Esad Landzo wound this fuse around Mrkajic, lit it and forced him to run round the hangar. I saw him when he poured petrol on the track suit of Dusko Bendjo forcing him to run around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "I saw him", whom did you see doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw when he did the same to these brothers, that is tied a fuse round their body and set light to it. To Risto Vukin too this was done by Esad Landzo in the presence of all the prisoners in the hangar. False executions were planned by Esad Landzo. He took Milan Djordjic outside the hangar. This one told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. He has no personal knowledge about what happened outside the hangar. He is talking about some false executions that he has no personal knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you please say exactly what you saw with your eyes? You saw Landzo taking outside ... go ahead. What did you see exactly with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my own eyes I saw Esad Landzo calling me personally out in front of the door of the hangar. All the prisoners saw this. He forced me no fall down on my knees and on that occasion he wanted to shoot me in the mouth but out of fear I couldn't open my mouth. Then with his gun he pressed it against my neck. I was terrified, but he took out the bullet and he -- where he leaned the gun against me, there was just the slight burn. I didn't feel much pain I was so terrified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. N, do you know a person named Mirko Vujcic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw when Esad Landzo with a kind of pincers, heated pincers, was burning his tongue. This was again in front of all the prisoners who were in the hangar at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say: approximately when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't give the exact date, but I know that all this happened after they tortured me and after he burnt me with a heated knife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Momir Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything particular concerning him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a blister on his hand from burning and he said that Esad Landzo had burnt him with a heated knife too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The blister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I mean, did you see the person who did that with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I saw the blister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you see when it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He did not see it. It was told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just saw him coming in the hangar and I saw the burn, and he said to all of us that Esad Landzo had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything because of direct knowledge about the circumstances of the death of any prisoner inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The death of Scepo Gotovac, an old man of 70, who was brought in. We had already been there for some time in the hangar, and one day Hazim Delic brought in the old man. I didn't know him personally until then. Later the people from Bjelovcina who were imprisoned with us said that his name was Scepo Gotovac. On that occasion Hasim Delic beat him in front of us several times. Then Esad Landzo came and took him out of the hangar. After that he was thrown back in. We heard cries for help and screams coming from Scepo and after a little time he died in the hangar amongst us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eyewitness anything else concerning people who died in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Simo Jovanovic was taken out in the same way as Scepo Gotovac outside the hangar, beaten up, brought back and he died there amongst us. Zeljko Cecez --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. N. What exactly did you see with your eyes concerning the incident of Simo Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already answered that he was taken out of the hangar, brought back and then he died.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I would like to know: did he see who took him out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A guard took him out. I don't know exactly his name. There were eyewitnesses who were close to the door. I personally don't know. They said it was Esad Landzo with a group of some people from the village of Idbar in the case of the death of Simo Jovanovic. I also forgot to say when Scepo Gotovac was thrown back into the hangar he had on his forehead a badge nailed in. I was not sure whether it was SDS or SDA badge. Esad Landzo personally had nailed this badge to his forehead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eyewitness any other incident concerning people who died in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Milorad Kuljanin was taken out of the hangar and on that occasion Esad Macic, Makaron, with another soldier -- I don't know his name -- he took Milorad Kuljanin out and they started beating him. That day was a Muslim religious holiday. On that occasion ten of us prisoners were going to the toilet behind the hangar, and when we passed by Milorad Kuljanin those who were in front, the four or five of them, they were forced to hit Milorad Kuljanin. Three or four men went by and Esad Macic, Makaron, pointed a gun at his forehead and fired two shots into his head directly. I was perhaps a metre or metre and a half away from the killed person, and I personally saw him firing the two bullets. On that occasion the first -- the man closest to the killed person was Zeljko Cecez and he was taken out that same evening and beaten for a whole hour in front of the hangar. He was thrown back in and a short while later that same evening he passed away in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eyewitness other incidents concerning people who died in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cedo Avramovic was found one morning dead at the end of the hangar. I don't know how death occurred, but I heard -- people were saying that he was afraid of the beating and probably had a heart attack, so I don't know. I am not sure. Bosko Samoukovic, Esad Landzo had come into the hangar and beaten Bosko Samoukovic with a plank, which was about a metre long. After that he took him out of the hangar and later Bosko Samoukovic was transferred to Building 22, where they tried to give him first aid, Dr. Relja and Petko, but later we learned that Bosko had died. Gojko Miljanic died in his son's arms in the hangar amongst us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this all you eyewitnessed concerning incidents regarding people who died in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember just now any others. Zeljko Klimenta, called Keljo, was taken out one morning about a quarter past five, and he was killed in front. Later, maybe about half an hour later, I saw his corpse behind the hangar and he was killed by somebody called Padalovic. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to Klimenta the day before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The day before Emir Kovacic came into the hangar, who was a friend of the late Keljo's, but Hazim Delic saw him in the hangar and shooed him away, telling him what he was doing there, and he said that he had brought some cigarettes for Keljo. Then Kovacic went out and came back and again he was found by Delic, and Delic told him to kiss him, that he would not see the day, to kiss him goodbye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did you observe Delic having in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic was Deputy Commander of the camp commander -- I am sorry. He was the Deputy Commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to know Mr. Delic's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found out Delic's name from people who worked with him together before the war, who were imprisoned together with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally know Mr. Delic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Esad Landzo from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time when Delic had some problem with his legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning -- in fact when we were brought to Number 22 Hazim Delic was a guard there for a while and I saw him walking on crutches, but personally I don't know what the reason for that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe Mr. Delic? I mean, what did he look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was tall. He had a large forehead. I don't think that I have to describe much. I can just look over to Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also there is not much need to describe him. I can just see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point him out then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Counting the people who are sitting there, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven -- I mean the sitting people on the bottom -- which number is Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two -- of the accused, I mean, excluding the policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted the record to be clear that he pointed out the second defendant, the second accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking from the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record to be clear, did you point out in this room both Mr. Landzo and Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, just for the record to be clear, can you exactly say which one is Landzo and which one is Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo is sitting number 3 persons sitting starting from the left and Mr. Delic is the first one from the far end. Maybe Mr. Landzo can get up so that he can be seen better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just for the record to be complete, we have also some ID done in the last few days through photo-spreads. Do you remember some days ago to have been shown a number of photos by an investigator in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked if you could recognise anybody in those photos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign some pieces of paper containing your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we start with this one. May I have, your Honour, this short statement with photo-spread attachment marked for identification as Number 93 and shown to the witness for identification purposes, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who are those you want him to identify?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is just because we did that in the last few days and defence lawyers received these photo-spreads, so for the completeness of the record I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who are those you want to identify? He can do it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is the defence disputing that he does not know the accused persons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In fact, you did not ask the relevant questions. Is this the same Landzo, the one you knew at the camp? Is it the same person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is the defence disputing he does not know those two accused persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. The only problem we have: in one of the photo-spreads you could not identify anybody. In court he identified my client. My client was on television. We are not disputing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are the ones he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey, are you disputing the witness does not know Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, he identified him in the photo-spread. We are not objecting to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The defence is not disputing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We are not disputing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So we withdraw the exhibition of this photo-spread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have gone about it in a roundabout way. In the beginning you could have linked it with who he knew at the camp. That's all you want to show, if this is the same Landzo he knew there. That would have satisfied it. This is the same Delic he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The accused persons have been appearing on the television. The identifications held a few days ago will not help you if the defence is not disputing. If the defence is not disputing, how would that help?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We withdraw these exhibits, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are not disputing it. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I would like to request, if possible, that Judge Jan, if possible, could cooperate by turning on the microphone, because we rely solely on the interpretation and we are very curious to know everything that the Trial Chamber is asking. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, if you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. N, do you have any knowledge of who was the Commander of the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zdravko Mucic called Pavo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that first from the guards and later from Hazim Delic, the deputy, because on several occasions when Pavo was to come to the hangar, Hazim Delic would tell us that the Commander was arriving, and then later I also saw when he released some people from the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times approximately did you see him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Two or three times at the most that I saw him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when you saw him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear a uniform?
